problem: Conventional assistive navigation for blind or visually impaired (BVI) users relies on localization, mapping and path planning with heavily hand-annotated semantic indoor maps aligned to sensor maps, which is costly and does not scale.
motivation: Humans navigate unfamiliar places through language instructions and visual scene understanding. A vision-language navigation (VLN) approach could remove the need for heavily labeled indoor maps, improving mobility, safety and independence for BVI individuals.
key_idea: Use a vision-language navigation model for global path inference on a scene-graph map, combined with a real-time obstacle-avoidance module for local navigation, deployed on an iPhone with cloud inference.
insight: From the abstract only: the style of the instruction matters for VLN success. Heuristic-style instructions outperform direction-style and detailed-style ones, and SR decreases as navigation length grows. No further ablation detail is available without the full text.
method: Scene-graph map construction module: builds a scene-graph map of the environment without heavy manual semantic annotation.
Navigation path generation module: performs global path inference using a VLN model given a language instruction.
Navigation with obstacle avoidance module: real-time local navigation and path re-planning around obstacles.
Deployment: runs on portable iPhone devices, with VLN model inference on cloud computing.

setting.observation: iPhone camera (likely RGB, possibly with depth/LiDAR; not stated)

numbers_note: abstract only; no quantitative values given
results: Field tests show the VLN global path finding and local path re-planning are effective. Heuristic-style instructions give higher VLN SR than direction or detailed instructions, and SR falls as path length increases. No numbers or baselines are reported in the abstract.
limitations: Success rate drops as navigation length increases.
Depends on cloud computing for VLN inference, so it needs connectivity and adds latency.
Evaluation appears limited to field tests, with no standard benchmark comparison stated.
